title: How Browsers Render a Page
objectives: Trace HTML and CSS into the DOM, the CSSOM and the render tree
Tell layout, paint and composite apart
Predict which change triggers which stage

cards.title: From bytes to pixels, stage by stage
cards.body: The browser parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM, combines them into a render tree of visible boxes, works out each box’s size and position (layout), fills in pixels (paint), then stacks painted layers on screen (composite).

cards.title: Misconception: the DOM is what you see
cards.body: The DOM holds every element, including ones with display: none, the head and script tags. Only the render tree decides what is drawn, so an element can be in the DOM and take no space on screen.

cards.title: One frame through the pipeline
cards.body: A style change runs only the stages after the one it touches. Changing width forces layout, paint and composite; changing colour skips layout; changing transform or opacity on its own layer can skip straight to composite.
steps: Style: match CSS rules to elements
Layout: compute size and position of each box
Paint: record drawing commands per layer
Composite: combine layers on the GPU into the frame

cards.title: Layers and the compositor thread
cards.body: Some elements are promoted to their own layer, for example while transform or opacity animates. The compositor can move such a layer without re-running layout or paint, which is why those animations stay smooth when the main thread is busy.

cards.title: Trap: reading layout in a write loop
cards.body: Changing a style and then reading an element’s size forces the browser to run layout immediately so it can answer. Doing that inside a loop forces layout once per iteration. Group the reads first, then the writes.

cards.title: Edge case: skipping work for off-screen sections
cards.body: content-visibility: auto lets the browser skip style, layout and paint for a section until it nears the viewport, which can cut the first render of long pages sharply. Pair it with contain-intrinsic-size so the skipped section keeps an estimated height; otherwise the scrollbar jumps as sections render.

questions.explanation: transform and opacity are the usual compositor-only properties; the others change layout.

questions.explanation: Reading geometry after a write forces synchronous layout; batch reads before writes.

questions.explanation: DOM and CSSOM feed the render tree; geometry comes before pixels, and layers are combined last.

flashcards.front: What does the render tree contain?
flashcards.back: Only the visible boxes: DOM nodes matched with their computed styles, minus things like display: none and <head>.

flashcards.front: Which stage computes size and position?
flashcards.back: Layout (also called reflow).

flashcards.front: Two properties that usually animate on the compositor?
flashcards.back: transform and opacity.

mechanism.title: What the browser does between receiving HTML and showing pixels
steps: Parsing: HTML is tokenised and built into the DOM tree incrementally, so the browser can start work before the whole file arrives. A preload scanner looks ahead for images, styles and scripts to fetch early.

Styles: CSS from link tags, style tags and inline styles is parsed into the CSSOM. CSS is render-blocking: the browser will not paint content until the stylesheets it already knows about have loaded, because painting with the wrong styles would cause a flash of unstyled content.

Render tree and style calculation: every visible DOM node gets its computed style. Nodes that are not rendered, such as head, script and anything with display: none, are left out. visibility: hidden stays in because it still takes space.

Layout: the browser walks the render tree and computes each box’s exact size and position from the viewport width down. A change high in the tree, such as the width of the body, can force layout for everything beneath it.
Paint: the browser records drawing commands (backgrounds, borders, text, shadows) for each layer and rasterises them into pixels, often in tiles.

Composite: layers are combined in the right order on screen, usually on the GPU and on a separate compositor thread. Scrolling and transform or opacity animations on promoted layers can update here without the main thread.

useWhen: Use transform and opacity for movement and fades so the compositor can do the work.
Batch DOM reads before writes when you must measure and then change many elements.
avoidWhen: Avoid promoting many elements to layers “just in case”: each layer costs memory and compositing time.
Avoid animating layout properties (width, height, top, left, margin) on large or complex pages.

numbers.title: The frame budget for a smooth animation
assumptions: The display refreshes 60 times per second (many phones and laptops; some screens are faster)
The browser needs part of each frame for its own housekeeping
steps: One frame lasts 1000 ms ÷ 60 ≈ 16.7 ms.
web.dev’s rendering guidance suggests aiming for roughly 10 ms of your own work per frame, leaving the rest for the browser.
A layout of a large page that takes 20 ms on a mid-range phone already overruns the frame, so the animation drops frames every time it runs.
Moving the same element with transform skips layout and paint, leaving only compositing, which fits easily.
numbers.result: At 60 Hz there is about 16.7 ms per frame; work that re-runs layout every frame is the usual reason an animation stutters.

india.title: Chrome DevTools Performance panel
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Browser developer tools show this pipeline directly. In a Performance recording, each frame is broken into purple “Layout” and “Recalculate Style” blocks, green “Paint” blocks and a “Composite Layers” step, and a warning flags forced reflows with the line of script that caused them. Recording a janky animation and seeing a tall purple Layout block in every frame is the most reliable way to confirm the cause before changing code.

pitfalls.trap: “The DOM is the page on screen.”
pitfalls.say: “The DOM is the document model; the render tree is what gets laid out and painted, and display: none nodes are not in it.”

pitfalls.trap: “Animations are slow because JavaScript is slow.”
pitfalls.say: “Most jank comes from re-running layout or paint each frame; I’d animate transform or opacity and check the Performance panel.”

takeaways: HTML becomes the DOM, CSS the CSSOM; together they form the render tree.
Layout computes geometry, paint draws pixels, composite stacks layers.
A change re-runs only the stages after the one it affects.
transform and opacity can animate on the compositor without layout or paint.

interactive.title: Fit the work in one frame
interactive.prompt: Your script, style and layout work takes 12 ms per frame. Change the screen’s refresh rate and see whether that work still fits in one frame.
interactive.takeaway: At 60 Hz a frame lasts about 16.7 ms, so 12 ms of work fits. At 90 Hz the frame is about 11.1 ms and the same work overruns it. Faster screens leave less time, so cutting layout and paint out of each frame matters more.

title: The Critical Rendering Path
objectives: Find the resources that block the first paint
Choose between blocking, defer and async scripts
Shorten the path to first content

cards.title: What blocks the first paint
cards.body: Stylesheets in the head are render-blocking: nothing paints until they load. A classic script tag is parser-blocking: HTML parsing stops while the script downloads and runs, because the script might change the document.

cards.title: Worked example: three requests before anything shows
cards.body: Each blocking resource the browser discovers late adds at least one round trip to the first paint.
steps: Assume: 100 ms round trip, HTML references one CSS file, the CSS imports a font stylesheet
Round trip 1: fetch the HTML
Round trip 2: the parser finds the CSS link and fetches it
Round trip 3: the CSS imports another stylesheet, fetched only now
cards.note: Result. About 300 ms of round trips before the first paint, plus connection setup and download time. Inlining critical CSS or linking both stylesheets from the HTML removes one round trip.

cards.title: How the three script modes load
cards.body: A classic script blocks the parser; defer downloads in parallel and runs in document order after parsing; async downloads in parallel and runs as soon as it arrives, in any order.
steps: Classic: stop parsing, download, run, resume
defer: download alongside parsing, run in order after the document is parsed
async: download alongside parsing, run immediately when ready
type=module: deferred by default

cards.title: Shortening the path
cards.body: Three levers: fewer critical resources (inline the small CSS needed above the fold, defer the rest), fewer bytes (minify, compress), and fewer round trips (reference critical files directly from the HTML so the preload scanner finds them early).

cards.title: Trap: async for scripts that depend on each other
cards.body: async scripts run in whatever order they finish downloading. If one script needs another, async can run them in the wrong order on a fast network one day and work the next. Use defer to keep document order.

cards.title: Edge case: an inline script waits for the stylesheet above it
cards.body: Because a script might read computed styles, browsers do not run any classic script while a stylesheet earlier in the document is still loading, whatever that script actually does. An inline script placed after a slow stylesheet therefore blocks the parser until that CSS arrives: the CSS has become parser-blocking too. Put such scripts before the stylesheet link, or defer them.

choices.label: The DOM cannot be built without CSS
CSS must run before JavaScript is downloaded
Painting without them would show unstyled content that then jumps
Stylesheets are always smaller than HTML

questions.explanation: CSS is render-blocking to avoid a flash of unstyled content; DOM construction itself continues.

choices.label: Inline it in the body before the content
defer with a dependency on the app bundle
async

questions.explanation: Independent scripts can run whenever they arrive; async avoids blocking the parser.

questions.prompt: Which change removes a round trip from the critical path?

choices.label: Serving the CSS from a different domain without preconnect
Moving the stylesheet link to the end of the body element
Adding a second, empty stylesheet to the head of the page

questions.explanation: An imported stylesheet is only discovered after its parent arrives; linking it from HTML lets the browser fetch both together.

items.label: Build the render tree and lay out
Parse HTML and discover the stylesheet

questions.explanation: The stylesheet blocks rendering, so its download sits on the path to the first paint.

assumptions: RTT 150 ms
Three sequential fetches: HTML, CSS, imported CSS
questions.explanation: Design implication: each nested import adds a full round trip, so on slow mobile links the import chain alone can delay first paint by about half a second. Flatten imports or inline the critical rules.

flashcards.back: CSS blocks rendering (painting); classic scripts block HTML parsing.
defer runs in document order after parsing; async runs as soon as each script arrives, in any order.
Deferred.

mechanism.title: How the browser decides it can paint
steps: The critical rendering path is the sequence of steps from receiving HTML to the first pixels: DOM, CSSOM, render tree, layout and paint. Anything that must finish before those steps can run sits on the path.

Critical resources are files that block the first render. By default these are the stylesheets in the head and classic scripts that appear before the content. Images do not block the first paint; they paint when they arrive.
A stylesheet with a media query that does not match (for example media="print") is still downloaded but does not block rendering. This is one way to keep non-critical CSS off the path.

Classic scripts block the parser because they may call document-writing functions or read styles. A classic script that comes after a stylesheet still loading waits for it, whatever the script reads (the HTML standard calls this a script-blocking style sheet), so CSS can indirectly delay scripts too.

The preload scanner reads ahead in the raw HTML and starts fetching resources it can see while the parser is blocked. Resources hidden inside CSS imports or injected by scripts are invisible to it and are discovered late.
Three numbers describe the path: how many critical resources there are, how many bytes they total, and how many round trips are needed to fetch them in sequence. Reduce any of them to paint sooner.

useWhen: Inline a small amount of critical CSS for above-the-fold content when the full stylesheet is large and the page is visited once.
Use defer for application scripts and async for independent third-party scripts.
avoidWhen: Avoid inlining large CSS on pages people visit repeatedly: inlined CSS cannot be cached separately and is re-downloaded with every HTML response.
Avoid async for scripts that rely on another script or on the full document being parsed.

rows: As soon as it is downloaded

numbers.title: Counting round trips on a slow connection
assumptions: Round trip 200 ms (an example slow mobile connection)
New connection to the origin: DNS, TCP and TLS add about 3 round trips once (example assumption)
HTML links two stylesheets directly; one script uses defer
steps: Connection setup: about 3 × 200 = 600 ms before the first byte of HTML can be requested.
HTML: one more round trip, about 200 ms.
Both stylesheets are found by the preload scanner and fetched in parallel: one round trip, about 200 ms.
The deferred script downloads in parallel but does not block the first paint.
numbers.result: Roughly 1 second before first paint under these assumptions, of which 600 ms is connection setup. Each extra sequential critical file would add another 200 ms.

india.title: Lighthouse “Eliminate render-blocking resources”
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Lighthouse, the auditing tool built into Chromium DevTools and documented on developer.chrome.com, has an audit that lists the stylesheets and scripts that delayed the first paint and estimates how much time each one cost. The usual fixes it suggests match this lesson: inline the critical styles, defer non-critical scripts, and mark stylesheets that only apply to print or large screens with a media attribute so they no longer block.

pitfalls.trap: “Put all scripts at the bottom and you are done.”
pitfalls.say: “Bottom-of-body scripts help, but defer lets the download start early without blocking, and I’d still count the critical CSS round trips.”

pitfalls.trap: “Async is always faster than defer.”
pitfalls.say: “async can run earlier, but it gives up ordering; for scripts that depend on each other defer is the safe choice.”

takeaways: CSS blocks rendering; classic scripts block parsing.
defer keeps order and runs after parsing; async runs on arrival.
Fewer critical resources, bytes and round trips mean an earlier first paint.
Resources hidden in CSS imports or scripts are discovered late.

interactive.title: Which script loading order is safe?
interactive.prompt: A page loads utils.js and app.js, and app.js calls functions defined in utils.js. Both are in the head with the async attribute. What happens?

choices.label: It works sometimes and breaks sometimes
choices.feedback: Right: async runs each file as soon as it arrives, so app.js can run first when it downloads faster.

choices.label: It always works because async keeps document order
choices.feedback: That is what defer does; async gives no ordering guarantee.

choices.label: It always fails because async scripts cannot share functions
choices.feedback: They share the global scope; the problem is only the order they run in.

interactive.reveal: async scripts execute in arrival order, not document order. Use defer for both (document order, after parsing), or load utils.js as a module that app.js imports.

title: The Browser Event Loop
objectives: Explain tasks, microtasks and rendering in one loop
Predict the order of callbacks
Keep long work from freezing the page

cards.title: One thread, one queue at a time
cards.body: The page’s scripts, event handlers and rendering share one main thread. The event loop takes one task (a click handler, a timer callback, a network response), runs it to completion, runs every queued microtask, then the browser may render a frame.

cards.title: Misconception: a zero-delay timer runs immediately
cards.body: A timer with a 0 ms delay only queues a task. It runs after the current script finishes and after all microtasks, such as resolved promise callbacks, so it is the last of the three in the example below.

cards.title: A single turn of the loop
cards.body: Rendering happens between tasks, never in the middle of one. A task that runs for 300 ms blocks clicks, typing and painting for all of that time.
steps: Take the oldest task from a task queue and run it
Run every microtask, including ones queued by microtasks
If a frame is due: run animation-frame callbacks, style, layout, paint
Repeat

cards.title: Breaking up long work
cards.body: A task longer than 50 ms counts as a long task. Split big loops into chunks and yield back to the loop between them, or move pure computation to a worker thread that has no access to the DOM.

cards.title: Trap: endless microtasks
cards.body: The loop drains the microtask queue completely before rendering. A promise callback that keeps queuing another promise callback never lets the browser paint or handle input, even though no single callback is long.

cards.title: Edge case: microtasks can starve rendering
cards.body: All microtasks queued during a task run before the browser may render, including microtasks queued by other microtasks. A promise chain that keeps scheduling more promise callbacks never gives the browser a chance to paint, even though no single callback is long. Break such loops into separate tasks so rendering can happen between them.

questions.prompt: A script logs A, then schedules a 0 ms timer whose callback logs B and queues a microtask that logs C. Next it resolves a promise whose callback logs D, and finally logs E. Output order?

choices.label: A, E, D, B, C
A, E, D, C, B
A, D, E, B, C
A, E, B, C, D

questions.explanation: The script runs to the end (A, E), then its microtask (D). The timer is the next task (B), and the microtask it queued runs straight after that task, before any later task (C).

questions.prompt: What counts as a long task in browser performance tooling?

choices.label: A task longer than one second
Any task that makes a network request
A task that runs longer than 50 ms
Any task that touches the DOM

questions.explanation: The Long Tasks definition uses 50 ms.

questions.prompt: When can the browser paint a new frame?

choices.label: Whenever a promise resolves
In the middle of any long-running function
Only after every timer has fired
Between tasks, after the microtask queue is empty

questions.explanation: Rendering is a step of the loop that runs between tasks.

choices.label: Wrap the parsing in a promise so it runs later

questions.explanation: Promises and timers still run on the main thread; a worker runs in parallel.

questions.explanation: Rendering steps come after the task and its microtasks.

The main thread stays free to handle input and paint

flashcards.back: Current synchronous code, then all microtasks, then the next task.
50 ms.

flashcards.front: Can a worker touch the DOM?
flashcards.back: No. It exchanges messages with the main thread.

mechanism.title: How the main thread schedules work
steps: A task is a unit of work the browser queues: parsing a chunk of HTML, dispatching a click, a timer firing, a message from a worker. The loop picks one task at a time and runs it to completion; nothing interrupts it.

Microtasks are smaller jobs queued during a task, mainly promise reactions and mutation observer callbacks. After each task, the loop runs every microtask, and any microtasks they queue, until the queue is empty.

Rendering is an opportunity, not a guarantee, in each turn. When the browser decides a frame is due (often about every 16.7 ms on a 60 Hz screen), it runs animation-frame callbacks, recalculates style, lays out and paints.

Timers are minimums, not exact times. A 0 ms timer waits for the current task and microtasks to finish, and browsers clamp nested timers to at least 4 ms after several levels of nesting, as the HTML standard specifies.

Input responsiveness depends on how long the main thread is busy. If a click arrives during a 400 ms task, its handler cannot start until that task finishes, and the screen cannot update until after that.
Workers run scripts on separate threads with their own event loops. They cannot touch the DOM; they post messages, which arrive on the main thread as tasks.

useWhen: Use workers for CPU-heavy work such as parsing, compression or large sorts.
Split long loops into chunks and yield between them so input and rendering can run.
avoidWhen: Avoid wrapping heavy synchronous work in a promise expecting it to run in the background; it still runs on the main thread.
Avoid chains of microtasks that requeue themselves; they starve rendering.

rows: Yes, if the queue never empties

numbers.title: How long a task can run before input feels slow
assumptions: web.dev’s responsiveness guidance treats about 100 ms as the point where a delay feels sluggish (the RAIL model)
A list of 10,000 items takes 0.03 ms each to process on a mid-range phone (an example assumption)
steps: Total work: 10,000 × 0.03 ms = 300 ms in one task.
A tap during that task waits up to 300 ms before its handler can even start.
Split into chunks of 1,000 items: each chunk takes 30 ms, under the 50 ms long-task threshold.
Yielding between chunks lets the tap run within one chunk, about 30 ms.
numbers.result: The same 300 ms of work, split into 30 ms chunks, keeps input delay near 30 ms instead of 300 ms.

india.title: Long tasks in DevTools
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Chromium DevTools marks every task longer than 50 ms with a red triangle in the Performance panel, and the Long Animation Frames API exposes similar information to monitoring scripts in the field. Teams use these markers to find which click handler or third-party script is blocking the main thread before reaching for a fix such as chunking the work or moving it to a worker.

pitfalls.trap: “Promises make code run in the background.”
pitfalls.say: “Promises schedule callbacks as microtasks on the same thread; CPU-heavy work still needs chunking or a worker.”

pitfalls.trap: “A 0 ms timer runs its callback right away.”
pitfalls.say: “It queues a task that runs after the current task and all microtasks, and possibly after a render.”

takeaways: One task runs to completion, then all microtasks, then maybe a render.
A 0 ms timer runs after promise callbacks.
Tasks over 50 ms are long tasks; split them or use a worker.
Workers run in parallel but cannot touch the DOM.

title: Rendering Models: CSR, SSR, SSG and Hydration
objectives: Say where HTML is produced in each model
Explain what hydration does and what it costs
Pick a model for a page’s freshness and interactivity

cards.title: Where the HTML comes from
cards.body: Client-side rendering (CSR) sends a near-empty page and builds the content in the browser with script. Server-side rendering (SSR) builds the HTML on the server for each request. Static site generation (SSG) builds the HTML once at build time and serves the same file to everyone.

cards.title: Misconception: server-rendered means interactive
cards.body: A server-rendered page can be visible before it responds to clicks. The script that attaches event handlers still has to download and run, so there is a gap between “looks ready” and “is ready”.

cards.title: What hydration does
cards.body: Hydration makes server-rendered HTML interactive by running the same components in the browser and attaching their behaviour to the existing markup instead of rebuilding it.
steps: Server sends full HTML and the state it used
Browser paints the HTML: content is visible
Script downloads and runs the components again
Event handlers attach: the page responds to input

cards.title: Choosing by freshness and audience
cards.body: Content the same for everyone and rarely changed (docs, marketing) suits static generation. Content per user or per request (a dashboard, search results) needs server rendering or client rendering. Highly interactive tools behind a login often accept client rendering because search engines do not need them.

cards.title: Trap: hydration mismatch
cards.body: If the browser’s first render differs from the server’s HTML, for example because it prints the local time or a random id, the framework must patch or discard that part of the page, and the user may see content flicker.

cards.title: Edge case: hydration mismatches
cards.body: Hydration expects the browser’s first render to produce the same markup as the server. Values that differ between the two, such as the current time, a random id, the user’s locale or anything read from browser storage, make the markup disagree. Frameworks then warn and re-render that part, losing the benefit of server rendering. Render such values after hydration or pass them from the server.

mechanism.title: What each rendering model does on each request
steps: Client-side rendering: the server returns a small HTML shell and one or more script bundles. The browser downloads and runs the script, which fetches data and builds the DOM. Nothing meaningful appears until that script has run.

Server-side rendering: for each request the server fetches data, renders the HTML and sends it. The browser can paint the content as soon as HTML and CSS arrive. To make it interactive the page usually also ships the script and hydrates.

Static site generation: the same rendering happens once at build time, producing HTML files that a CDN can serve directly. Changing content means rebuilding the affected pages (some tools rebuild individual pages on a schedule).

Hydration: the browser re-runs the components against the existing HTML so their state and handlers attach to it. It costs downloading and executing roughly the same script as client rendering, so it improves when content appears but not necessarily when it becomes interactive.
Streaming and partial approaches reduce that cost: the server can stream HTML in chunks, and some approaches hydrate only the interactive “islands” of a page, leaving static parts as plain HTML.
The choice is per page, not per site: a marketing page can be static, a product page server-rendered and a logged-in editor client-rendered.

useWhen: Static generation for content that is the same for everyone and changes rarely.
Server rendering when content is per request but must be visible fast and indexable.
avoidWhen: Avoid client-only rendering for pages whose first visit and search ranking matter, such as landing pages.
Avoid shipping a large hydration bundle for a mostly static page; plain HTML with small scripts is cheaper.

numbers.title: Where the time goes on a slow phone
assumptions: Example: 300 KB of compressed script
Download at 1.6 Mbit/s (an example slow mobile connection)
Parse and run the bundle: 1.5 s on a mid-range phone (example assumption)
steps: Download: 300 KB × 8 = 2,400 kbit; 2,400 ÷ 1,600 kbit/s ≈ 1.5 s.
CSR: content appears only after download and execution, about 1.5 + 1.5 = 3 s plus HTML and data fetches.
SSR: content is visible once HTML arrives, before the 3 s of script work.
With hydration, the page still becomes interactive only after roughly the same 3 s.
numbers.result: Server rendering moves when content appears much earlier; when it becomes interactive still depends on the script size.

Its central point matches this lesson: server rendering and static rendering show content sooner, but hydration can leave a page that looks ready while it still ignores input, so the size of the script shipped to the browser still matters.

pitfalls.trap: “SSR makes the page interactive sooner.”
pitfalls.say: “SSR makes content visible sooner; interactivity still waits for the script and hydration.”

pitfalls.trap: “Pick one rendering model for the whole site.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d choose per page: static for docs, server-rendered for search results, client-rendered for the logged-in editor.”

Hydration attaches behaviour to server-rendered HTML and costs the script download and run.
Visible and interactive are different moments.
Choose per page by freshness, personalisation and search needs.

title: Browser HTTP Caching
objectives: Read Cache-Control, ETag and Last-Modified
Tell no-cache from no-store
Design a caching policy for HTML and versioned assets

cards.title: Fresh, stale and revalidated
cards.body: A cached response is fresh until its max-age runs out. While fresh, the browser uses it without asking the server. Once stale, the browser revalidates: it asks “has this changed?” and gets either a new copy or a short 304 Not Modified.

cards.title: Misconception: no-cache means do not cache
cards.body: no-cache allows storing the response but requires revalidation before every use. The directive that forbids storing it at all is no-store.

cards.title: A conditional request with an ETag
cards.body: The ETag is a version label for the response. Revalidation sends it back so the server can answer with headers only.
steps: First response: 200, Cache-Control: max-age=60, ETag: "v7"
After 60 s the copy is stale
Browser sends If-None-Match: "v7"
Unchanged: server replies 304 with no body; the browser reuses its copy

cards.title: Versioned file names
cards.body: Put a content hash in asset file names (app.3f9a1c.js) and serve them with a long max-age and immutable. When the file changes, its name changes, so browsers fetch the new one. Keep the HTML that references them short-lived or revalidated.

cards.title: Trap: long-lived HTML
cards.body: Caching the HTML for a day while assets change names means returning visitors keep loading yesterday’s HTML, which points at yesterday’s asset names. Short or no-cache HTML plus long-lived hashed assets avoids this.

cards.title: Edge case: caching without any Cache-Control
cards.body: A response with a Last-Modified date but no explicit freshness can still be cached: RFC 9111 lets caches assign a heuristic lifetime, and suggests a typical value of 10% of the time since the resource was last modified. A file unchanged for 30 days might then be reused for about 3 days without asking. Always send explicit Cache-Control on responses whose freshness matters.

no-store

Cache-Control: "a1"

questions.explanation: If-None-Match carries the ETag; If-Modified-Since carries a date.

An error the browser must retry

questions.explanation: The point of 304 is to skip re-sending the body.

questions.explanation: Revalidation turns a full download into a header-only exchange.

no-store everywhere is fastest for repeat visits

flashcards.back: no-cache: store but revalidate before use. no-store: do not store.
ETag with If-None-Match; Last-Modified with If-Modified-Since.
So a long max-age is safe: new content gets a new URL.

sources.title: web.dev: Prevent unnecessary network requests with the HTTP Cache

mechanism.title: How the browser decides to reuse a response
steps: When a response is stored, the browser computes its freshness lifetime: from max-age in Cache-Control if present, otherwise from Expires. With neither, RFC 9111 lets caches use a heuristic, commonly a fraction (such as 10%) of the time since Last-Modified, which is why unlabelled responses are sometimes cached unexpectedly.
While the response is fresh, the browser serves it from cache with no network request at all. That is the fastest case and the one long max-age values on hashed files aim for.

When it is stale, the browser makes a conditional request using the stored validators: If-None-Match with the ETag, or If-Modified-Since with the Last-Modified date. The server compares and replies 304 Not Modified with headers only, or 200 with the new body.

Directives refine this: no-cache requires revalidation before every use; no-store forbids storing; private allows the browser but not shared caches (CDNs, proxies) to store it; public allows shared caches; immutable tells the browser not to revalidate while fresh, even on reload.
The cache key is mainly the URL (with the method). Vary lists request headers, such as Accept-Encoding, that also select a stored copy, so different variants do not overwrite each other.
A practical policy for web apps: HTML with no-cache (or a short max-age) and an ETag; versioned assets with max-age=31536000, immutable; personal API responses with private or no-store.

useWhen: Long max-age with immutable for any file whose URL contains a content hash.
no-cache plus an ETag for HTML and other files that keep the same URL but change.
avoidWhen: Avoid long max-age on URLs whose content changes without the URL changing; users keep the old version until it expires.
Avoid no-store on static assets; it throws away the cheapest performance win.

numbers.title: What revalidation saves
assumptions: HTML page 60 KB compressed (example)
A 304 response is about 300 bytes of headers (example)
Round trip 100 ms; link 10 Mbit/s
steps: Full download: 60 KB × 8 = 480 kbit ÷ 10,000 kbit/s ≈ 48 ms of transfer plus 100 ms round trip ≈ 150 ms.
304: one round trip of 100 ms plus negligible transfer.
Fresh cache hit with max-age: no request at all, close to 0 ms of network time.
For a 2 MB script: full download ≈ 1.6 s at 10 Mbit/s, versus 0 ms when served fresh from cache.
numbers.result: Revalidation saves bandwidth but still costs a round trip; a fresh hit costs nothing, which is why hashed assets get long lifetimes.

india.title: MDN’s recommended caching pattern
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The MDN guide to HTTP caching describes the same pattern under “cache busting”: give the main HTML a policy that forces revalidation, and give versioned JavaScript and CSS files a long max-age with immutable so browsers never ask about them again. The pattern is widely used by build tools that append content hashes to file names at build time.

pitfalls.trap: “Set no-cache so users never see stale content.”
pitfalls.say: “no-cache still stores; it revalidates each use. no-store is the one that stops storing.”

pitfalls.trap: “Just cache everything for a day.”
pitfalls.say: “Hashed assets can be cached for a year; HTML should revalidate so a deploy is visible on the next visit.”

takeaways: Fresh responses are reused without a request; stale ones are revalidated.
no-cache revalidates; no-store does not store.
ETag + If-None-Match turns a re-download into a 304.
Hashed assets: long max-age, immutable. HTML: revalidate.

interactive.title: What does the browser do?
interactive.prompt: Yesterday the browser stored style.css with Cache-Control: no-cache and ETag "v3". The file has not changed. The user opens the page again.

choices.feedback: Right: no-cache means revalidate before use, and an unchanged file gives a 304.

choices.label: Downloads the whole file again
choices.feedback: It has a validator, so it asks first and gets a short 304.

choices.label: Uses the stored copy without asking
choices.feedback: That would happen with a max-age that had not expired, not with no-cache.

interactive.reveal: no-cache permits storing but forbids using the copy without checking. The ETag makes that check cheap: a 304 with headers only.

title: Browser Storage: Cookies, Web Storage, IndexedDB
objectives: Compare cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage and IndexedDB
Set cookie attributes for a session cookie
Pick storage by size, lifetime and who needs to read it

cards.title: Four places to keep data
cards.body: Cookies are small and sent with every matching request. localStorage and sessionStorage are simple string key-value stores read only by scripts on the same origin. IndexedDB is an asynchronous database in the browser for larger, structured data.

cards.title: Misconception: localStorage is a safe place for tokens
cards.body: Any script running on the page can read localStorage, including one injected through an XSS bug. An HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by scripts at all, which limits what an injected script can steal.

cards.title: Setting a session cookie safely
cards.body: The attributes on Set-Cookie decide who can read the cookie and when it is sent.
steps: HttpOnly: scripts cannot read it
Secure: sent only over HTTPS
SameSite=Lax or Strict: not sent on most cross-site requests
Path and Max-Age: where it applies and how long it lives

cards.title: Sizes and lifetimes
cards.body: Browsers keep at least 4 KB per cookie (RFC 6265 sets that as a minimum to support). Web storage is usually limited to about 5 MiB per origin. IndexedDB can use far more, subject to the browser’s storage quota. sessionStorage ends with the tab; the others persist until cleared or expired.

cards.title: Trap: large cookies on every request
cards.body: Cookies ride on every request to their domain, including requests for images and scripts. Storing a few kilobytes of preferences in cookies adds those bytes to each request, so keep cookies to identifiers and keep bulk data in client storage.

cards.title: Edge case: browsers may delete script-written storage
cards.body: WebKit documented in 2020 that Safari deletes all script-writable storage (localStorage, IndexedDB, service worker registrations) for a site after seven days of browser use without user interaction with that site. Treat client storage as a cache that can disappear, and keep the source of truth on the server.

choices.label: Max-Age
Secure
SameSite=None
HttpOnly

IndexedDB

sessionStorage

A token in localStorage
An HttpOnly session cookie

questions.explanation: About 4 KB, about 5 MiB, then a share of disk.

constraints: Must limit damage from a script injection bug
Server is on the same site

questions.explanation: A hardened cookie keeps the credential out of reach of scripts while still surviving reloads.

localStorage persists; sessionStorage ends with the tab.

flashcards.front: Storage for large structured offline data?
flashcards.back: IndexedDB (asynchronous, quota-managed).

mechanism.title: How each storage option behaves
steps: Cookies are set by the server with Set-Cookie (or by script, unless HttpOnly) and sent back in the Cookie header on matching requests. Domain and Path decide which requests match; Expires or Max-Age decides lifetime; without them the cookie lasts for the browser session.

SameSite controls cross-site sending. Strict never sends on cross-site requests; Lax sends on top-level navigations such as following a link but not on cross-site sub-requests or form POSTs; None sends everywhere but requires Secure. Chromium-based browsers treat a cookie without SameSite as Lax.

localStorage and sessionStorage store strings per origin (scheme, host and port). Calls are synchronous, so large reads and writes can block the main thread. sessionStorage is also scoped to a single tab.

IndexedDB stores structured objects and binary data with indexes and transactions. Its API is asynchronous, so it does not block rendering, and it can hold far more data, within the quota the browser grants the origin.

All client storage is under the user’s control and can be cleared or evicted under storage pressure (unless persistence is granted). Treat it as a cache, never as the only copy of something the user cannot lose.

Anything a script can read, an injected script can read. Keep credentials out of web storage when an HttpOnly cookie is an option, and never store secrets in client storage that the user should not see.

useWhen: Cookies for session identifiers the server must receive on each request.
IndexedDB for offline data, large caches and structured records; web storage for small preferences.
avoidWhen: Avoid putting bulk data in cookies; it is uploaded with every request.
Avoid storing access tokens in localStorage when the app can use an HttpOnly cookie instead.

numbers.title: The cost of cookies on every request
assumptions: A page makes 80 requests to the same domain (HTML, scripts, images, API calls)
Cookies on that domain total 3 KB (an example)
Mobile upload speed 1 Mbit/s (example)
steps: Extra upload per page view: 80 × 3 KB = 240 KB.
240 KB × 8 = 1,920 kbit, about 1.9 s of upload time at 1 Mbit/s if sent serially (HTTP/2 header compression reduces repeats).
Serving static files from a cookieless domain avoids sending the cookies with them.
Keeping cookies to a session id of a few dozen bytes makes the overhead negligible.
numbers.result: Kilobytes of cookies multiplied by dozens of requests add up; keep cookies small and keep bulk data in client storage.

india.title: Chromium’s SameSite=Lax default
india.label: Public documentation
india.body: In 2020 Chrome began treating cookies without a SameSite attribute as SameSite=Lax and rejecting SameSite=None cookies that are not also Secure, as documented on chromium.org and web.dev. Sites that relied on cookies being sent in cross-site POSTs, such as some payment and login callbacks, had to set SameSite=None; Secure explicitly. Other browsers have their own defaults, so set the attribute explicitly rather than relying on any default.

pitfalls.trap: “localStorage is fine for tokens because it is per origin.”
pitfalls.say: “Per origin still means every script on the page, including injected ones; I’d use an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie.”

pitfalls.trap: “Client storage is permanent.”
pitfalls.say: “Browsers can evict it and users can clear it; it is a cache, and the server holds the source of truth.”

takeaways: Cookies travel with requests; web storage and IndexedDB stay in the browser.
HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite harden session cookies.
Web storage is small, synchronous and string-only; IndexedDB is large and asynchronous.
Anything scripts can read, injected scripts can read too.

interactive.reveal: SameSite=Lax blocks the cookie on cross-site sub-requests and POSTs, which removes the classic CSRF form attack. Strict also blocks it on cross-site link clicks. Keep CSRF tokens for older browsers and same-site attackers.

title: Same-Origin Policy and CORS
objectives: Decide whether two URLs share an origin
Explain simple requests and preflights
Configure CORS for credentials safely

cards.title: What counts as the same origin
cards.body: An origin is the scheme, host and port together. https://shop.example and https://api.shop.example are different origins, and so are http:// and https:// versions of one host. Scripts can read responses only from their own origin unless the other origin opts in.

cards.title: Misconception: CORS protects your server
cards.body: CORS is enforced by the browser on behalf of the user, and it controls whether a page’s script may read a response. The request can still reach your server, and tools outside a browser ignore CORS entirely. Authentication and CSRF protection still need their own checks.

cards.title: A preflighted request
cards.body: For requests that are not “simple”, the browser asks permission first with an OPTIONS request.
steps: Script on https://app.example sends PUT with a JSON body to https://api.example
Browser sends OPTIONS with Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT and the requested headers
Server replies with Access-Control-Allow-Origin, -Methods, -Headers (and optionally Max-Age)
If allowed, the browser sends the real PUT; otherwise the script gets an error

cards.title: Which requests skip the preflight
cards.body: Simple requests use GET, HEAD or POST, only safelisted headers, and a Content-Type of form encoding, multipart form data or plain text. A JSON body or an Authorization header makes the request non-simple, so a preflight is sent first.

cards.title: Trap: a wildcard origin with credentials
cards.body: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * cannot be combined with credentials (cookies or HTTP authentication). Echoing back any Origin header with Allow-Credentials: true lets every website read logged-in users’ data. Allow a fixed list of origins instead.

cards.title: Edge case: CORS answers cached by a CDN
cards.body: If an API echoes the caller’s Origin in Access-Control-Allow-Origin but omits Vary: Origin, a shared cache can store the response for one origin and serve it to another. The second front end then sees intermittent CORS errors that depend on which origin warmed the cache. Send Vary: Origin whenever the CORS headers depend on the request.

questions.prompt: Which pair has the same origin?

choices.label: https://site.example and https://www.site.example
https://site.example/a and https://site.example:443/b
https://site.example:8443 and https://site.example
http://site.example and https://site.example

choices.label: A GET with no custom headers
A HEAD request
A POST with a form-encoded body
A POST with Content-Type: application/json

questions.prompt: A server returns no CORS headers. What happens when a cross-origin page sends a simple POST to it?

choices.label: The server rejects it automatically with a 403 error
The browser never sends the request to the server at all
The response is readable, but cookies are stripped from it
The request reaches the server, but the page’s script cannot read the response

Allow-Origin: https://app.example and Allow-Credentials: true
Allow-Origin: * and Allow-Credentials: true
Allow-Credentials: true without Allow-Origin

questions.explanation: Credentials require an explicit origin; browsers reject the wildcard.

items.label: Browser gives the response to the script
Script asks the browser to send PUT to another origin
Browser sends OPTIONS with the requested method and headers
Server answers with the allowed origins, methods and headers

questions.explanation: Permission first, then the real request.

constraints: Third-party sites must not read user data

approaches.label: Allow-Origin: * with credentials
Echo any Origin with credentials
Check Origin against an allowlist and echo it back, with credentials and Vary: Origin

rationaleOptions.label: Reflecting every Origin is safe because cookies are SameSite
Only listed origins can read credentialed responses
Vary: Origin stops caches from serving one origin’s headers to another

rationaleConflicts.r3: SameSite does not cover every case (same-site subdomains, older browsers), and reflecting all origins opens the data to any site.

questions.explanation: An allowlist plus Vary: Origin is the standard safe configuration for credentialed CORS.

flashcards.back: Scheme + host + port.
For non-simple requests: other methods, non-safelisted headers, or a content type such as JSON.
No; browsers reject it. Use an explicit origin.

mechanism.title: How the browser enforces origins and CORS
steps: The same-origin policy restricts how a document or script from one origin interacts with resources from another. Embedding is mostly allowed (images, scripts, stylesheets, iframes); reading cross-origin responses from script and reaching into another origin’s DOM are not.

CORS is a protocol in the Fetch standard that lets a server relax that rule for specific origins. The browser adds an Origin header to cross-origin requests and checks the response headers before handing the response to the script.

Simple requests (GET, HEAD or POST with safelisted headers and content types) are sent directly. If the response lacks a matching Access-Control-Allow-Origin, the browser blocks the script from reading it, but the server has already processed the request.

Other requests are preflighted with OPTIONS, carrying Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers. The server answers with what it allows; Access-Control-Max-Age lets the browser cache that answer for a while.

Credentialed requests (cookies, HTTP authentication) need the script to opt in and the server to respond with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true and an explicit origin, never *. Responses that vary by Origin should send Vary: Origin so shared caches keep them apart.
CORS errors are deliberately vague in scripts for security; the browser console shows the real reason. Testing with a command-line client will not reproduce them, because only browsers enforce CORS.

useWhen: Use an explicit allowlist of origins when an API serves a few known front ends.
Serve the front end and API from the same origin (for example behind one reverse proxy) to avoid CORS entirely.
avoidWhen: Avoid reflecting any Origin back with credentials; it makes user data readable by every site.
Avoid treating CORS as access control; authenticate and authorise every request on the server.

rows: Safe if the list is tight
Any site can read user data

numbers.title: What preflights cost
assumptions: Round trip 120 ms between the user and the API (example)
A page makes 10 different non-simple API calls on load
No Access-Control-Max-Age is set
steps: Each call needs an OPTIONS round trip before the real request: 10 × 120 ms = 1.2 s of extra round trips if made one after another.
With Access-Control-Max-Age: 600, the browser reuses the preflight result for 10 minutes for the same URL and method (browsers cap this value: Chromium at 2 hours, Firefox at 24 hours).
Serving the API from the same origin removes the preflights entirely.
Requests made in parallel overlap their preflights, but each still adds at least one round trip to its own latency.
numbers.result: Preflights can add one round trip per call; caching them with Max-Age or using one origin removes most of that cost.

india.title: The Fetch standard
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: CORS is specified in the WHATWG Fetch standard, which every major browser implements. It defines exactly which methods, headers and content types are “CORS-safelisted”, how preflight results are cached, and why the wildcard origin is refused for credentialed requests. When a browser’s behaviour seems surprising, the Fetch standard and MDN’s CORS guide are the places to check rather than blog posts.

pitfalls.trap: “CORS stops attackers calling my API.”
pitfalls.say: “CORS only stops other sites’ scripts from reading responses in a browser; I still authenticate requests and defend against CSRF.”

pitfalls.trap: “Just set Allow-Origin to * and Allow-Credentials to true.”
pitfalls.say: “Browsers reject that combination; I’d allow an explicit list of origins and add Vary: Origin.”

takeaways: Origin is scheme + host + port.
Simple requests are sent; CORS decides whether script can read the response.
Non-simple requests are preflighted with OPTIONS.
Credentials need an explicit origin, never *.

choices.feedback: Different hosts are different origins, even on one site.

interactive.reveal: A request is simple only if its method, headers and content type are all on the safelist. Adding Authorization means the browser sends OPTIONS first.

Apply output encoding and a Content Security Policy
Stop forged requests with SameSite cookies and tokens

cards.title: Two attacks with similar names
cards.body: Cross-site scripting (XSS) gets the attacker’s script to run inside your page, with all the user’s access. Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) makes the user’s browser send a request to your site from another site, carrying the user’s cookies, without running any script on your page.

cards.title: Misconception: input filtering stops XSS
cards.body: Stripping “<script>” from input misses event handler attributes, URLs with script schemes and many encodings. The reliable defence is encoding output for the exact place it is inserted (HTML text, attribute, URL, script) when rendering.

cards.title: How a stored XSS plays out
cards.body: The attack starts as data and becomes code only when a page renders it without encoding.
steps: Attacker posts a comment containing markup with an event handler
Server stores it unchanged
Another user opens the page; the comment is inserted as raw HTML
The handler runs in that user’s session and can act as them

cards.title: Defence in depth for XSS
cards.body: Encode output by context, prefer APIs that set text rather than HTML, sanitise only where rich HTML is truly needed, and add a Content Security Policy that blocks inline scripts and limits script sources, so a missed bug is harder to exploit.

cards.title: Trap: a CSRF token in a GET link
cards.body: State-changing actions sent as GET requests can be triggered by an image tag on another site, and tokens in URLs leak through logs and the Referer header. Make state changes use POST (or other non-GET methods) with a token in the body or a header.

cards.title: Failure story: a modified script on a payment page
cards.body: Publicly reported: in 2018 attackers altered JavaScript served on British Airways’ booking pages so that card details typed into the payment form were also sent to an attacker-controlled domain. The UK Information Commissioner’s Office reported that data of more than 400,000 customers and staff was affected and fined the airline £20 million in 2020. Defences: Subresource Integrity on third-party scripts, a CSP that limits where scripts may send data (connect-src), and monitoring for changed script files.

questions.prompt: Which attack needs the attacker’s code to run inside your page?

choices.label: Clickjacking
A brute-force login attempt
Cross-site request forgery
Cross-site scripting

questions.explanation: XSS runs script in your origin; CSRF only causes a request.

questions.prompt: A user’s display name is inserted into an HTML page. What is the main defence?

choices.label: Reject any display name longer than 20 characters
Strip the word “script” from the input before saving
Store the name in a cookie instead of the page
Encode it for HTML when rendering, so markup characters show as text

questions.explanation: Context-aware output encoding is the core XSS defence.

questions.prompt: Which defence stops a hidden cross-site form from transferring money with the user’s cookie?

choices.label: Making the transfer endpoint respond with JSON
HTML-encoding every field shown in the transfer form
A per-session CSRF token the server checks on every state change
A Content Security Policy on the bank’s own pages

questions.explanation: The attacker’s page cannot read the token, so the forged request fails the check.

questions.prompt: What does a Content Security Policy add if an encoding bug slips through?

choices.label: It encrypts the page so scripts cannot read it
It replaces server-side validation
It blocks all cross-site requests
It can stop inline and unlisted scripts from running

questions.explanation: CSP limits which scripts execute, reducing the impact of an injection.

questions.prompt: Order a classic CSRF attack.

items.label: The browser attaches the bank cookie
User logs in to the bank; a session cookie is stored
The page auto-submits a hidden form to the bank
The bank acts on the request as the user

questions.explanation: SameSite cookies or a CSRF token break the chain at step four or five.

questions.prompt: A forum must let users post comments with bold, italics and links.
constraints: Comments are shown to other users

approaches.label: Insert the comment HTML as written
Strip the word “script” and insert the rest
Sanitise with an allowlist of tags and attributes, plus a strict CSP

rationaleOptions.label: A CSP limits damage if the sanitiser misses something
An allowlist keeps only known-safe tags and attributes
Blocking the word script stops all script execution

rationaleConflicts.r3: Event handler attributes and script URLs run code without any script tag.

questions.explanation: When rich HTML is needed, use a maintained allowlist sanitiser and back it with a CSP.

flashcards.back: Attacker-controlled script runs in your page.
Another site makes the user’s browser send a request to yours with their cookies.
Context-aware output encoding (plus CSP as a second layer).

sources.title: OWASP: Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet

mechanism.title: How each attack works and where each defence acts
steps: Reflected XSS: input in a request (for example a search term) is echoed straight into the response page. Stored XSS: the input is saved and shown to other users later. DOM-based XSS: the page’s own script copies data from the URL or storage into the page as HTML.

In every XSS variant, data crosses into a code context. Output encoding keeps it data: in HTML text, < becomes <; in an attribute, quotes are encoded; in a URL, only safe schemes are allowed; inside script, data goes through a safe serialiser rather than string concatenation.

Sanitisation is a different tool: it parses untrusted HTML and keeps only allowed tags and attributes. Use a maintained library for it when users must submit rich text; do not write your own with regular expressions.

A Content Security Policy is a response header listing where scripts, styles and other resources may come from. A strict policy using nonces or hashes blocks inline event handlers and injected script tags, which turns many XSS bugs into failed attempts.

CSRF relies on the browser attaching cookies automatically. Defences make a forged request distinguishable: SameSite cookies stop them being attached cross-site; a synchroniser token (a random value the page includes and the server checks) cannot be read by the attacking site; checking the Origin header rejects requests from unexpected sites.
XSS defeats CSRF defences: script running in your page can read the token and send requests itself. Fix XSS first; CSRF protection assumes your own page is not compromised.

useWhen: Context-aware output encoding everywhere data is rendered, plus a strict CSP as a safety net.
SameSite cookies plus CSRF tokens (or Origin checks) on every state-changing request.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on input blacklists to stop XSS.
Avoid state changes on GET requests; links and images can trigger them from any site.

numbers.title: How small the attack surface needs to be
assumptions: A page renders 40 pieces of user data in different places (example)
1 in 40 output sites is mis-encoded by hand (illustrative)
steps: Expected encoding bugs per page: 40 × 1/40 = 1.
One missed encoding is enough for XSS, so relying on manual escaping at each insertion point does not scale.
Using rendering that encodes by default (templates or APIs that set text) moves the risk to the few places that deliberately insert HTML.
A strict CSP adds a second barrier for those few places.
numbers.result: With dozens of insertion points, auto-encoding by default plus CSP is far safer than escaping each one by hand.

india.title: The OWASP cheat sheets
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, maintained by the Open Worldwide Application Security Project, is the standard reference for these defences. Its XSS prevention sheet is organised by output context (HTML body, attribute, URL, script, CSS) because the right encoding depends on where data lands. Its CSRF sheet recommends synchroniser tokens or signed double-submit cookies, with SameSite cookies as defence in depth rather than the only control.

pitfalls.trap: “We sanitise input, so we are safe from XSS.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d encode on output for each context and add a CSP; input filtering misses event handlers and encodings.”

pitfalls.trap: “CORS protects us from CSRF.”
pitfalls.say: “CORS controls reading responses; a forged form POST is still sent. SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens address CSRF.”

takeaways: XSS runs attacker script in your page; CSRF forges requests with the user’s cookies.
Encode output for its context; use CSP as a second layer.
SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens stop forged requests.
XSS bypasses CSRF defences, so fix XSS first.

interactive.title: Which defence fits?
interactive.prompt: Your banking site has an endpoint that transfers money on POST. An attacker controls an unrelated website and can make visitors’ browsers submit forms. Pick the defence that targets this attack.

choices.label: A CSRF token checked on the transfer endpoint, plus SameSite cookies
choices.feedback: Right: this is CSRF; the attacker can make requests but cannot read your token.

choices.label: A Content Security Policy on the bank’s pages
choices.feedback: CSP limits scripts on your pages; the attack comes from another site’s form.

choices.label: HTML-encoding the transfer amount on the confirmation page
choices.feedback: Encoding stops XSS; this attack does not inject script.

interactive.reveal: Name the attack first. Forged cross-site requests are CSRF; the defences are SameSite cookies plus a token or Origin check on state-changing requests.

title: Web Accessibility Fundamentals
objectives: Use semantic HTML so assistive tech understands the page
Make every action work by keyboard with visible focus
Check text alternatives, labels and colour contrast

cards.title: The accessibility tree
cards.body: Browsers build an accessibility tree from the DOM: each element’s role (button, link, heading), name (its label) and state (expanded, checked). Screen readers and voice control read that tree, so the right element gives the right role for free.

cards.title: Misconception: ARIA fixes everything
cards.body: The first rule of ARIA use in the W3C guidance is to prefer a native HTML element when one exists. A div with role="button" still needs focusability, Enter and Space handling and a visible focus style written by hand; a button element has all of that built in.

cards.title: Checking a page by keyboard
cards.body: Unplug the mouse and try the main tasks. Each step finds a common failure.
steps: Tab: every interactive control is reachable in a logical order
Focus: you can always see where you are
Enter or Space: buttons and links activate
Escape: dialogs close and focus returns to where it was

cards.title: Text alternatives, labels and contrast
cards.body: Informative images need alt text describing their purpose; decorative ones need empty alt so they are skipped. Every form field needs a programmatic label. WCAG level AA asks for 4.5:1 contrast for normal text and 3:1 for large text.

cards.title: Trap: hint text as the only label
cards.body: Hint text shown inside an empty field disappears as soon as someone types, is often low contrast, and is not reliably announced as a label. Keep a visible label element tied to the field and use in-field hint text only for an example value.

cards.title: Edge case: aria-label on a plain div or span
cards.body: ARIA 1.2 does not allow naming generic elements: aria-label on a div or span without a role is ignored by many screen readers. The label only works on elements with a role that supports a name, such as a button, link, image or region. Use the right native element first; add ARIA to fill gaps, not to decorate generic containers.

questions.prompt: You need a clickable control that submits a form. What should you use?

choices.label: A span styled to look like a button
A native button element
A div with role="button" and a click handler
A link with href="#"

questions.explanation: Native elements bring role, focus and keyboard behaviour for free.

questions.prompt: What contrast ratio does WCAG AA require for normal-size body text?
questions.explanation: 3:1 applies to large text; 7:1 is the stricter AAA level.

questions.prompt: A decorative divider image adds nothing to the meaning. What alt text should it have?

choices.label: alt="decorative divider image"
An empty alt attribute (alt="")
alt="image"
No alt attribute at all

questions.explanation: Empty alt tells assistive tech to skip it; a missing alt may cause the file name to be read.

questions.prompt: A modal dialog opens. What should happen to keyboard focus?

choices.label: Jump to the first link on the page, then into the dialog
Move into the dialog, stay there while open, and return to the trigger on close
Move to the browser address bar until the dialog closes
Stay on the page behind the dialog so users can keep reading

questions.explanation: Otherwise keyboard and screen-reader users are left behind the dialog.

questions.prompt: Order a quick accessibility check of a new page.

items.label: Check images and fields have names
Check headings form a sensible outline

questions.explanation: Structure, keyboard, focus, names, then visual checks.

questions.prompt: A custom dropdown menu built from divs fails keyboard testing.

approaches.label: Use native elements (a button and a list of links or a select) and style them
Add role attributes to the divs and stop
Hide it from assistive tech

rationaleOptions.label: Role attributes add keyboard support automatically
Styling native elements is usually less work than rebuilding their behaviour
Native elements come with keyboard handling and roles

rationaleConflicts.r3: ARIA changes what is announced, not how the element behaves.

questions.explanation: ARIA describes; it does not add behaviour. Native elements are the cheapest accessible option.

flashcards.back: Prefer a native HTML element with the semantics you need.
4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text.

flashcards.front: Alt text for a decorative image?
flashcards.back: Empty: alt="".

sources.title: W3C: Using ARIA (rules of ARIA use)

mechanism.title: How assistive technology understands a page
steps: The browser exposes an accessibility tree alongside the DOM. Each node has a role, an accessible name and states. A button element is exposed as role button, named by its text; a heading as level 2 heading; a checkbox with its checked state.
Screen readers navigate by those roles: jump between headings, landmarks (header, nav, main), links or form fields. A page built from divs gives them nothing to jump to, even if it looks fine.
Accessible names come from content, a label element, alt text or ARIA attributes. Every interactive element and informative image needs one; a button that contains only an icon needs a text name.

Keyboard access depends on focusable elements. Native links, buttons and form fields are focusable and respond to Enter or Space. Custom widgets need tabindex, key handlers and focus management, which is why native elements are preferred.

WCAG (the W3C’s Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) groups success criteria into levels A, AA and AAA. Many laws and procurement policies reference level AA, which includes the 4.5:1 contrast rule, keyboard operability and visible focus.
Automated checkers catch missing alt text, labels and contrast problems, but not whether alt text is meaningful or a flow makes sense; manual keyboard and screen-reader testing is still needed.

useWhen: Semantic HTML first for headings, lists, buttons, links, forms and landmarks.
ARIA for widgets HTML has no element for, such as tabs, following the ARIA authoring practices.
avoidWhen: Avoid removing focus outlines without a visible replacement.
Avoid conveying information by colour alone, such as red fields with no text error.

rows: Role, tabindex, key handlers, focus style

numbers.title: Checking a colour pair for contrast
assumptions: Text #767676 on white #FFFFFF (an example pair)
WCAG relative luminance: white is 1.0; #767676 works out to about 0.181
steps: Contrast ratio = (lighter + 0.05) ÷ (darker + 0.05).
4.54 is at least 4.5, so this grey just passes AA for normal text.
A slightly lighter grey such as #777777 drops just below 4.5:1 and fails.
numbers.result: Mid greys on white sit right at the AA boundary, so check the ratio rather than judging by eye.

india.title: WCAG 2.2 and its adoption
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: WCAG 2.2 became a W3C Recommendation in October 2023, adding criteria such as a minimum target size for pointer inputs and making focused elements not entirely hidden by sticky headers. Many public-sector accessibility rules reference WCAG level AA, for example the European standard EN 301 549 that public bodies in the EU follow. Checking against AA is therefore a practical baseline for most products.

pitfalls.trap: “We added ARIA labels everywhere, so it is accessible.”
pitfalls.say: “ARIA only changes what is announced; I’d start with native elements, then test by keyboard and with a screen reader.”

pitfalls.trap: “Automated tools passed, so we are compliant.”
pitfalls.say: “Automated checks catch a minority of issues; keyboard and screen-reader testing find the rest.”

takeaways: Native HTML elements give roles, names and keyboard support for free.
Prefer native elements to ARIA; ARIA does not add behaviour.
Everything must work by keyboard with visible focus.
AA contrast: 4.5:1 normal text, 3:1 large text.

interactive.title: What does a screen reader announce?
interactive.prompt: An icon-only close button is written as a div with a click handler and an X icon, and nothing else.

choices.label: Nothing useful: it is not focusable, has no role and no name
choices.feedback: Right: a div is not a control, and the icon has no text name.

choices.label: “Close button”, from the X icon
choices.feedback: The icon gives no accessible name, and a div has no button role.

choices.label: “Button”, because it has a click handler
choices.feedback: Click handlers are not exposed as roles.

interactive.reveal: Use a button element with an accessible name, such as visually hidden text or aria-label="Close". It becomes focusable, is announced as “Close, button” and works with Enter and Space.

title: Web Performance Metrics: LCP, INP, CLS
objectives: Define LCP, INP and CLS and their “good” thresholds
Tell field data from lab data
Name the usual fix for each metric

cards.title: Three questions, three metrics
cards.body: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) asks “did the main content load quickly?”. Interaction to Next Paint (INP) asks “does the page respond quickly to input?”. Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) asks “does content stay put?”.

cards.title: Misconception: a fast lab score means fast for users
cards.body: A lab test runs one device on one network. Field data comes from real visits on many devices and networks, and Core Web Vitals are judged at the 75th percentile of those visits. A page can score well in the lab and still fail in the field.

cards.title: The good thresholds, at the 75th percentile
cards.body: A page passes when at least 75% of visits meet each threshold.
steps: LCP: 2.5 s or less
INP: 200 ms or less
CLS: 0.1 or less
Poor starts above 4 s, 500 ms and 0.25 respectively

cards.title: What usually fixes each one
cards.body: LCP: fetch the main image or text sooner and remove render-blocking work. INP: shorten long tasks in event handlers and render less after input. CLS: reserve space for images, ads and embeds with width and height or aspect ratios, and avoid inserting content above what the user is reading.

cards.title: Trap: lazy-loading the hero image
cards.body: Marking the largest above-the-fold image as lazy delays its request until layout decides it is visible, which pushes LCP later. Lazy-load images below the fold and let the main image load eagerly, even with a high fetch priority.

cards.title: Edge case: what INP does not see
cards.body: INP counts clicks, taps and key presses. Scrolling and hovering are not interactions for INP, and a visit with no interactions has no INP value at all. A page can therefore feel janky while scrolling yet pass INP; check scroll smoothness separately in the Performance panel.

questions.prompt: Which metric measures how quickly the page responds to clicks and key presses?

choices.label: Interaction to Next Paint (INP)
Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)
Time to First Byte (TTFB)

questions.explanation: INP replaced First Input Delay as the responsiveness Core Web Vital in March 2024.

questions.prompt: What is the “good” LCP threshold?

choices.label: 1 second
200 milliseconds
4 seconds
2.5 seconds

questions.explanation: 4 s is where “poor” begins; 200 ms is the INP threshold.

questions.prompt: At what percentile of page visits are Core Web Vitals assessed?

choices.label: The 75th percentile
The 95th percentile
The median (50th)
The single fastest visit

questions.explanation: The 75th percentile balances typical and slower experiences.

questions.prompt: Text jumps down when a banner ad loads above it. Which fix targets this?

choices.label: Lazy-load the article text below the banner
Compress the ad image to a smaller file
Load the ad script with the async attribute
Reserve the ad slot’s height before the ad loads

questions.explanation: CLS comes from unreserved space; reserving it stops the shift.

questions.prompt: Order the three parts of one interaction’s latency, as INP measures it.

items.label: Presentation delay: style, layout and paint of the next frame
Input delay: the main thread finishes what it was doing

questions.explanation: INP spans from the input to the next painted frame, so all three parts count.

questions.prompt: 1,000 page views have LCP values; 780 are at or below 2.5 s. Does the page pass LCP? Enter the percentage of visits within the threshold.
assumptions: 1,000 field visits
780 at or below 2.5 s
questions.explanation: Sanity check: passing needs at least 75% of visits within the threshold, so 78% passes, but only just; a slower network week could tip it under.

flashcards.front: Good thresholds for LCP, INP, CLS?

flashcards.back: 75th percentile of real visits.
Reserve space: width/height or aspect-ratio on media and slots.

mechanism.title: How each metric is measured
steps: LCP is the time from navigation start until the largest image or text block in the viewport is rendered. It is usually a hero image, a video poster or a headline. Delays come from slow server responses, render-blocking resources, late discovery of the image, or a large image download.

INP observes all clicks, taps and key presses during a visit and reports roughly the worst latency from input to the next frame being painted (ignoring a few outliers on pages with many interactions). Each interaction includes input delay (main thread busy), processing time (event handlers) and presentation delay (rendering the update).

CLS adds up unexpected layout shifts: each shift scores the fraction of the viewport that moved multiplied by how far it moved. Shifts within 500 ms of user input do not count. Shifts are grouped into windows and the worst window is reported.

Field data comes from real users, for example through the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX) or your own monitoring with the web-vitals library. Lab data comes from controlled tests such as Lighthouse. Use lab data to debug and field data to judge.
Each metric is assessed at the 75th percentile of page loads, separately for mobile and desktop. A page passes the Core Web Vitals assessment when all three meet their “good” thresholds.
The metrics are related to work covered in earlier lessons: LCP depends on the critical rendering path and caching, INP on the event loop, and CLS on layout.

useWhen: Use field data to decide whether there is a problem and lab tools to find its cause.
Track the 75th percentile per page type, on mobile and desktop separately.
avoidWhen: Avoid optimising for a single lab score on a fast developer machine.
Avoid fixing LCP by hiding content until everything loads; it makes the experience worse.

rows: Slow server, render-blocking CSS, late or large hero image
Long tasks in event handlers, heavy re-rendering
Media without dimensions, late-inserted banners, web fonts swapping

numbers.title: Scoring one layout shift
assumptions: A banner pushes an article down after load (illustrative)
The shifted article covers 60% of the viewport height before and after the move combined (impact fraction 0.6)
It moves down by 25% of the viewport height (distance fraction 0.25)
steps: Layout shift score = impact fraction × distance fraction.
0.15 is above the 0.1 “good” threshold from this one shift.
Reserving the banner’s height in advance makes the shift score 0.
numbers.result: One late banner can fail CLS on its own; reserving space removes the shift entirely.

india.title: The move from FID to INP
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: In March 2024 Google replaced First Input Delay (FID) with Interaction to Next Paint (INP) as the responsiveness Core Web Vital, as announced on web.dev. FID measured only the delay before the first interaction’s handler started; INP covers all interactions and includes handler time and the time to paint the result. Many sites that passed FID failed INP at first, mostly because of long tasks in event handlers.

pitfalls.trap: “Our Lighthouse score is 95, so performance is fine.”
pitfalls.say: “Lighthouse is a lab test on one profile; I’d check field data at the 75th percentile on mobile.”

pitfalls.trap: “Lazy-load every image to improve LCP.”
pitfalls.say: “Lazy-loading the hero image delays LCP; I’d lazy-load below-the-fold images only.”

takeaways: LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1, judged at the 75th percentile.
Field data judges; lab data debugs.
INP is about long tasks in handlers; CLS about reserving space.
Never lazy-load the LCP image.

interactive.title: Which metric does this hurt?
interactive.prompt: A product page’s “Add to cart” click handler recalculates prices for 2,000 variants on the main thread, taking 350 ms before the button shows its new state.

choices.label: INP
choices.feedback: Right: input to next paint takes at least 350 ms, above the 200 ms “good” threshold.

choices.label: LCP
choices.feedback: LCP is about when the main content first renders, not about clicks.

choices.label: CLS
choices.feedback: Nothing moves unexpectedly here.

interactive.reveal: Interactions that run long tasks on the main thread delay the next paint. Show the button’s pressed state first, then do the heavy work in chunks or a worker.
