title: Loading Assets Efficiently
objectives: Use resource hints and fetch priority on purpose
Serve right-sized, compressed images and text
Lazy-load and split code without delaying what matters

cards.title: Send fewer, smaller bytes, sooner
cards.body: Asset loading comes down to three moves: discover critical files early, make every file as small as it can be, and delay anything that is not needed for the first view.

cards.title: Worked example: one hero image, three sizes
cards.body: Serving a phone the desktop image wastes most of its bytes.
steps: Assume: a hero shown 400 CSS px wide on a phone with a device pixel ratio of 2
The phone needs about 800 px wide; the desktop file is 2,400 px wide
Pixels scale with width squared: (2,400 ÷ 800)² = 9× more pixels than needed
With srcset offering 800, 1,600 and 2,400 px versions, the browser picks the 800 px file
cards.note: Result. Roughly a ninth of the pixels to decode, and usually a similar cut in bytes, for the same sharpness on that phone.

cards.title: Hints that change when things load
cards.body: Resource hints tell the browser about work it would otherwise discover late.
steps: preconnect: open the connection to a third-party origin early
preload: fetch a specific critical file now (a font, the hero image)
fetchpriority="high": raise one image above others
loading="lazy": wait until an image or iframe is near the viewport

cards.title: Compression and code splitting
cards.body: Text assets (HTML, CSS, scripts, JSON) compress well with gzip or Brotli. Splitting scripts by route means a visitor downloads the code for the page they opened, not the whole application.

cards.title: Trap: preloading everything
cards.body: Every preload competes for bandwidth with the files the browser already knows are critical. Preloading many files can delay the hero image or the main stylesheet. Preload one or two late-discovered critical files and measure.

cards.title: Edge case: the hero image found too late
cards.body: A hero image set as a CSS background, or inserted by script, is invisible to the preload scanner and is fetched only after CSS or JavaScript runs, which delays LCP. Use an img element in the HTML with fetchpriority="high", or a preload hint, and never mark it loading="lazy".

questions.prompt: A web font is referenced only inside a stylesheet, so it is discovered late. Which hint helps?

choices.label: preload the font file
preconnect to your own origin
fetchpriority="low" on the stylesheet
font-display: swap in the @font-face rule

questions.explanation: preload starts the fetch before the CSS that references it is parsed.

questions.prompt: What does srcset with width descriptors let the browser do?

choices.label: Download every listed size and keep the sharpest
Convert each image to a newer format on the fly
Pick the smallest file that is sharp enough for the layout and screen
Lazy-load the image automatically when offscreen

questions.explanation: The browser chooses using the sizes attribute and device pixel ratio.

questions.prompt: Which images should use loading="lazy"?

choices.label: The site logo in the header
Images well below the fold
Every image on the page
The hero image at the top

questions.explanation: Lazy-loading above-the-fold images delays them.

questions.prompt: Which asset gains least from gzip or Brotli on the server?

choices.label: A JavaScript bundle
An HTML page
A JPEG photo
A JSON API response

questions.explanation: JPEG, PNG and WebP are already compressed; text formats shrink a lot.

questions.prompt: Order these by how early they should load on a product page.
questions.explanation: The HTML and critical CSS come first and below-the-fold extras last. The hero image and the add-to-cart script both serve the first view, so either order between them is accepted.

questions.prompt: A marketing page loads a 400 KB chat widget script on every visit.
constraints: Chat is used by 3% of visitors
Chat must still work when opened

approaches.label: Load it synchronously in the head
Preload it with high priority
Load the widget only when the visitor clicks the chat button

rationaleOptions.label: 97% of visitors never download the 400 KB
The first view’s critical resources no longer compete with it
Preloading makes the widget cheaper to download

rationaleConflicts.r3: Preload changes timing, not size, and steals bandwidth from critical files.

questions.explanation: Load rarely used features on interaction; keep the critical path for what every visitor needs.

flashcards.back: preconnect opens a connection to an origin; preload fetches a specific file.

flashcards.front: When not to lazy-load an image?
flashcards.back: When it is above the fold, especially the LCP image.
Text: HTML, CSS, scripts, JSON, SVG. Not JPEG/PNG/WebP.

mechanism.title: How the browser schedules and sizes downloads
steps: The browser assigns each request a priority: render-blocking CSS and fonts high, scripts by type and position, images low until layout shows they are in the viewport. Hints and attributes adjust these defaults.
preconnect performs DNS, TCP and TLS for an origin ahead of time, saving those round trips when the first request to it happens. Use it for a few critical third-party origins, such as an image CDN.

preload fetches a specific URL with a stated type immediately and keeps it ready. It suits files the HTML does not mention directly, such as fonts referenced from CSS or a background hero image. An unused preload wastes bandwidth and triggers a console warning.

Responsive images give the browser options: srcset lists candidate files and their widths, sizes says how wide the image will be in the layout, and the browser picks the best match for the screen. Modern formats such as WebP and AVIF are usually smaller than JPEG at similar quality; picture with source elements offers them with a fallback.
Native lazy loading (loading="lazy") defers offscreen images and iframes until they approach the viewport. Width and height attributes still matter so the layout reserves space and does not shift.
For scripts, split the bundle by route and load rarely used features on demand. Compress text responses with Brotli or gzip, and cache hashed files for a long time so repeat visits skip the download.

useWhen: Preload one or two late-discovered critical files such as the LCP image or a primary font.
Serve responsive images in a modern format with dimensions set.
avoidWhen: Avoid preloading large numbers of files; it dilutes priorities.
Avoid lazy-loading anything visible in the first viewport.

rows: Saves connection round trips to a third party
Starts a late-discovered critical file early
Steals bandwidth from other critical files
Delays LCP if applied to the hero

numbers.title: How much compression saves on a script
assumptions: A 900 KB minified JavaScript bundle (example)
Text like this often compresses to about a quarter to a third of its size with Brotli (an illustrative ratio; measure your own)
Link 5 Mbit/s
steps: Uncompressed: 900 KB × 8 = 7,200 kbit ÷ 5,000 kbit/s ≈ 1.4 s.
At a quarter of the size, 225 KB: 1,800 kbit ÷ 5,000 ≈ 0.36 s.
Compression does not cut parse and execution time; the browser still processes 900 KB of code.
Splitting so the first page needs only 300 KB of code cuts both transfer and execution time.
numbers.result: Compression cuts transfer time, but only shipping less code cuts execution time too.

india.title: Native lazy loading in browsers
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The loading attribute for images and iframes is part of the HTML standard and supported in all major browsers. web.dev’s guide explains that browsers start fetching lazy images some distance before they scroll into view, with the distance depending on connection speed, and warns specifically against lazy-loading images in the initial viewport because doing so delays LCP.

pitfalls.trap: “Preload all our fonts and images so they are ready.”
pitfalls.say: “Preloading everything competes with the critical files; I’d preload only the LCP image or primary font and measure.”

pitfalls.trap: “Gzip solves our big bundle.”
pitfalls.say: “Compression cuts bytes on the wire, not parse and execution time; I’d split the bundle by route.”

takeaways: Discover critical files early, shrink every file, delay the rest.
Responsive images send the right pixels for each screen.
Preload and preconnect sparingly; lazy-load below the fold only.
Compress text; split code so the first view needs less.

interactive.title: Size or round trips?
interactive.prompt: A page needs a script bundle after 4 round trips of 100 ms on a 5 Mbit/s mobile link. Slide the compressed bundle size and see which part of the wait dominates.
interactive.takeaway: Below about 0.25 MB the 400 ms of round trips dominate, so preconnect and fewer sequential requests help most. Above it the bytes dominate: 1 MB alone takes 1.6 s at 5 Mbit/s, so code splitting and compression matter more.

title: Forms and Validation
objectives: Split validation between browser and server correctly
Show errors people and assistive tech can find
Prevent duplicate submissions and lost input

cards.title: Two layers, two jobs
cards.body: Validation in the browser is for the user: fast feedback before a round trip. Validation on the server is for the system: it is the only check an attacker cannot skip, because requests can be sent without your page at all.

cards.title: Misconception: the browser already checked it
cards.body: Constraint attributes such as required, type="email", min and pattern can be removed in developer tools, and scripts or command-line clients can post anything. Treat every field as untrusted on the server, even if the form validated it.

cards.title: One submission, done well
cards.body: A form that behaves well on slow networks follows the same few steps.
steps: Validate in the browser on submit; focus the first invalid field
Disable the submit button and show progress
Server validates again and saves, using an idempotency key
Success: redirect to a result page (Post/Redirect/Get)
Failure: show field errors next to the fields and keep the input

cards.title: Errors people can find
cards.body: Put each error message in text next to its field, associate it with the field so screen readers announce it, and summarise errors at the top for long forms. Never rely on a red border alone.

cards.title: Trap: refresh resubmits the order
cards.body: If a successful POST returns a page directly, pressing refresh asks to send the POST again. Redirecting to a GET page after success (Post/Redirect/Get) makes refresh safe; an idempotency key on the server catches the remaining double clicks and retries.

cards.title: Edge case: what maxlength counts
cards.body: The HTML maxlength attribute counts UTF-16 code units, so many emoji count as 2, while a server may count bytes (UTF-8: up to 4 per character) or user-visible characters. A 20-character limit can then pass in the browser and fail on the server. Define the limit in one unit, enforce it on the server, and show the same rule in the form.

questions.prompt: Which validation can an attacker not bypass?

choices.label: Validation on the server
The required attribute
A script that checks fields before submit
A pattern attribute

questions.explanation: Everything in the browser is under the user’s control.

questions.prompt: After a successful POST, what stops a page refresh from submitting again?

choices.label: Returning the result page directly from the POST
Redirecting to a GET result page (Post/Redirect/Get)
Adding a required attribute to every field
Setting the form to autocomplete="off"

questions.explanation: Refreshing a GET page does not resend the form.

questions.prompt: How should a field error be shown?

choices.label: In a pop-up that closes after two seconds
As a red border only
Only in the browser console
As text next to the field, programmatically linked to it

questions.explanation: Text tied to the field reaches screen-reader users and people who cannot see colour.

questions.prompt: A user double-clicks “Pay” on a slow connection. Which server-side measure prevents a double charge?

choices.label: A pattern attribute on the amount field in the form
Returning 200 OK for both of the requests
Validating the card number twice before charging
An idempotency key sent with the request and checked by the server

questions.explanation: The second request with the same key returns the first result instead of charging again.

questions.prompt: Order a robust form submission.

items.label: Disable the button and show progress

questions.explanation: Feedback first, the authoritative check on the server, then a safe redirect.

questions.prompt: Sign-up form: username must be unique and 3–20 characters.
constraints: Two people may pick the same name at once

approaches.label: Only check on the server, no browser checks
Only check uniqueness in the browser by calling an API while typing
Length check in the browser, plus a unique constraint enforced on the server

rationaleOptions.label: Only a server-side unique constraint closes the race between two sign-ups
The browser gives instant feedback on length
A browser availability check guarantees uniqueness

rationaleConflicts.r3: Two users can both see “available” and submit; only the server constraint decides.

questions.explanation: Browser checks improve experience; the server enforces the rule, including races.

flashcards.front: Why validate on the server if the browser does?
flashcards.back: Requests can bypass the browser; the server is the only enforceable check.
After a successful POST, redirect to a GET page so refresh does not resubmit.
Next to its field, linked programmatically, not colour alone.

mechanism.title: How a form submission travels and where each check belongs
steps: HTML has built-in constraint validation: required, type (email, url, number), min, max, minlength, maxlength and pattern. On submit the browser blocks invalid forms and shows a message, and scripts can read each field’s validity state to show custom messages instead.

Choose input types for the job: type="email" and type="tel" bring suitable on-screen keyboards on phones, autocomplete attributes let browsers fill known values, and inputmode tunes the keyboard without changing validation.

On the server, validate every field for type, length, range and format, then apply business rules (the username is free, the coupon is valid). Use allowlists where possible. Return errors per field in a structured form so the page can show them next to the right input.

Uniqueness and similar invariants belong in the database as constraints. A browser check that a username is “available” is a hint; two people can submit the same name at the same moment, and only the constraint settles it.

A submit can be sent twice by double clicks, retries on a flaky network or refresh. Disable the button while sending, follow Post/Redirect/Get after success, and accept an idempotency key so the server can return the first result for a repeated request.

Errors must be perceivable by everyone: text next to the field, linked with an attribute such as aria-describedby, focus moved to the first invalid field, and the user’s input kept so they can fix rather than retype it.

useWhen: Browser constraints for quick feedback on format and required fields.
Server validation and database constraints for every rule that must hold.
avoidWhen: Avoid clearing the whole form when one field fails.
Avoid relying on in-field hint text or colour alone to explain errors.

rows: Feedback in the browser; enforcement on the server
Retries and double clicks come from the client

numbers.title: How often double submissions happen
assumptions: A checkout gets 20,000 orders a day (illustrative)
0.5% of payments see a retry or double click while the first request is in flight (illustrative)
steps: Expected repeat submissions: 20,000 × 0.005 = 100 per day.
Without idempotency, each could become a duplicate charge or order.
Disabling the button stops most double clicks but not network retries.
An idempotency key makes all 100 return the original result.
numbers.result: Even a small retry rate means dozens of duplicates a day at modest volume; the server must make repeats harmless.

india.title: Payment APIs and idempotency keys
india.label: Public documentation
india.body: Several public payment APIs document an Idempotency-Key request header: the client generates a unique key per intended operation and resends the same key on retries, and the server returns the stored result of the first request instead of performing the action again. The IETF has a draft standard for this header. A form submission can use the same idea by generating the key when the form is rendered.

pitfalls.trap: “The form validates emails, so the server can trust the field.”
pitfalls.say: “Anything in the browser can be bypassed; the server validates every field again.”

pitfalls.trap: “We disable the button, so duplicates cannot happen.”
pitfalls.say: “Disabling helps with double clicks; retries and refreshes still need Post/Redirect/Get and an idempotency key.”

takeaways: Browser validation is for users; server validation is for the system.
Uniqueness belongs in a database constraint.
Post/Redirect/Get plus idempotency keys make repeats harmless.
Show errors as text next to fields and keep the input.

interactive.title: What happens when the user refreshes?
interactive.prompt: A payment form POSTs to /pay, and the server responds with the receipt page directly (status 200). The user presses refresh on the receipt.

choices.label: The browser offers to send the POST again, which could pay twice
choices.feedback: Right: refreshing a page that came from a POST repeats the POST.

choices.label: The receipt reloads safely with a GET
choices.feedback: That is what happens after a redirect to a GET page, not here.

choices.label: Nothing: browsers never resend forms
choices.feedback: Browsers ask to resend form data on refresh after a POST.

interactive.reveal: Post/Redirect/Get: respond to a successful POST with a redirect (303 See Other) to a receipt URL. Refresh then repeats a harmless GET. Keep an idempotency key on the server for retries.

title: Client State and Data Fetching
objectives: Tell server state from UI state
Avoid stale and out-of-order responses
Choose optimistic or confirmed updates

cards.title: Two kinds of state
cards.body: UI state belongs to the page: which tab is open, what is typed in a field. Server state is a copy of data owned elsewhere: the cart, the user’s messages. Server state can go stale, so it needs fetching, caching and refreshing rules; UI state does not.

cards.title: Misconception: the last request sent wins
cards.body: Responses can arrive in a different order from requests. If a search for “ca” is slow and “cat” is fast, showing whichever arrives last can display results for “ca” under the “cat” box.

cards.title: Searching as you type, safely
cards.body: A search box needs to ignore answers to questions the user is no longer asking.
steps: Wait briefly after typing stops (debounce)
Send the request and remember its query
When a newer query starts, cancel or mark older requests stale
Render a response only if it matches the latest query

cards.title: Optimistic updates
cards.body: An optimistic update changes the screen before the server confirms, then rolls back if the request fails. It suits likes, toggles and reordering, where failure is rare and easy to undo; it does not suit payments or anything whose result the user must be able to trust.

cards.title: Trap: copying server data into many places
cards.body: Storing the same user record in several components means an update to one copy leaves the others stale. Keep one cache entry per resource and let views read from it.

cards.title: Edge case: two components ask for the same data at once
cards.body: When a header and a sidebar both request the current user as the page loads, a naive cache misses twice and sends two identical requests. Data-fetching layers keep a map of in-flight requests by key and give the second caller the same pending result, which removes duplicate requests and keeps both components consistent.

questions.prompt: Which of these is server state?

choices.label: Text typed in a search box before submit
The list of items in the user’s saved cart
Which tab is selected
Whether a dropdown is open

questions.explanation: It is owned by the server and can change elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Search for “ca” returns after the search for “cat”. What should the page show?

choices.label: An error, because responses arrived out of order
Results for “cat”, ignoring the late “ca” response
Results for “ca”, because it arrived last
Both result lists merged

questions.explanation: Only render responses that match the current query.

questions.prompt: Which action suits an optimistic update?

choices.label: Toggling a “like” on a post
Deleting an account permanently
Placing a stock order
Submitting a bank transfer

questions.explanation: Likes are low-risk and easy to roll back.

questions.prompt: What does debouncing a search box do?

choices.label: Waits until typing pauses before sending a request
Sends one request per key press
Retries failed requests automatically
Sends at most one request per second

questions.explanation: It cuts requests for intermediate keystrokes.

questions.prompt: Order an optimistic “like” update.

items.label: On failure, roll back the count and tell the user

questions.explanation: Show first, confirm after, undo on failure.

questions.prompt: Updating a shared to-do list item’s “done” checkbox.
constraints: Other users may edit the same list

approaches.label: Wait for the server before ticking the box
Update locally and never confirm
Optimistic update with rollback, then refresh from the server

rationaleOptions.label: Local-only updates are fine because the server will catch up
The box ticks instantly and is corrected on the rare failure
Refetching reconciles changes made by other users

rationaleConflicts.r3: Without sending and confirming, the server never learns of the change.

questions.explanation: Low-risk toggles suit optimistic updates, as long as failures roll back and data is refreshed.

flashcards.back: UI state lives in the page; server state is a cached copy of data owned elsewhere.
Track the latest request; cancel or ignore older ones.

flashcards.front: When are optimistic updates a bad idea?
flashcards.back: When the user must trust the result, such as payments.

sources.title: MDN: Using the Fetch API (cancelling requests)

mechanism.title: How client code keeps a copy of server data honest
steps: Classify state before choosing where to keep it. UI state (open panels, form drafts, scroll position) is owned by the page. Server state (records, lists, counts) is owned by the server; the page only holds a snapshot that ages from the moment it arrives.

For server state, the useful questions are: what is the key for this data (for example user 42’s profile), how long is the copy fresh, when is it refetched (on focus, on reconnect, after a mutation), and who else reads it.
One cache entry per key, shared by every view, avoids copies drifting apart. After a change, update or invalidate that entry, and every view that reads it shows the new value.

Requests can overlap and complete in any order. Keep an identifier for the latest request per key, and cancel older ones (browsers provide an abort mechanism for in-flight requests) or discard their responses when they arrive.

Optimistic updates write the expected result into the cache immediately, send the request, and on failure restore the previous value and tell the user. Pessimistic (confirmed) updates show progress and change the screen only after the server agrees.
Conditional requests (ETag and If-None-Match) make refetching cheap: unchanged data returns a 304 with no body, so refreshing on focus does not have to cost a full download.

useWhen: Optimistic updates for small, reversible actions where speed matters.
A single shared cache keyed by resource for server data used in several views.
avoidWhen: Avoid optimistic updates for payments, irreversible actions or anything with complex server-side rules.
Avoid duplicating server data into many independent component states.

numbers.title: How many requests debouncing saves
assumptions: A user types a 12-character query at about 5 characters per second
Without debouncing, one request per keystroke
Debounce: send 300 ms after typing pauses (an example value)
steps: Without debouncing: 12 requests, most for partial words.
Typing gaps are about 200 ms, below 300 ms, so the debounce fires once at the end.
With debouncing: 1 request (plus any during longer pauses).
That is roughly a 90% cut in requests and in out-of-order responses to handle.
numbers.result: Debouncing turns a dozen requests into about one; cancellation handles the few that still overlap.

india.title: Request cancellation in the platform
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The DOM standard defines an abort signal, documented on MDN, that lets a page cancel an in-flight request. Search boxes and typeahead components use it to cancel the previous request when a new query starts, which both saves bandwidth and removes the out-of-order response problem at its source. The same signal can cancel timers and event listeners tied to a view that has closed.

pitfalls.trap: “The latest response is always for the latest request.”
pitfalls.say: “Responses can arrive out of order; I track the latest request and ignore or cancel older ones.”

pitfalls.trap: “Make every update optimistic for speed.”
pitfalls.say: “Only for low-risk, reversible actions; payments and deletes wait for the server.”

takeaways: UI state is the page’s; server state is a cached copy that goes stale.
Keep one cache entry per resource and invalidate it on change.
Debounce and cancel to avoid out-of-order responses.
Optimistic updates suit small, reversible actions only.

interactive.title: Which results appear?
interactive.prompt: A search box sends a request on every keystroke and renders whichever response arrives. The user types “ca”, then “cat”. The “ca” request takes 900 ms; the “cat” request takes 200 ms.

choices.label: “cat” results flash, then are replaced by “ca” results
choices.feedback: Right: the slow “ca” response lands last and overwrites the correct results.

choices.label: Only “cat” results, because it was sent last
choices.feedback: Send order does not decide arrival order.

choices.label: Only “ca” results, because it was sent first
choices.feedback: “cat” arrives first and is shown briefly before being overwritten.

interactive.reveal: Render only responses that match the current query, and cancel superseded requests. Debouncing reduces how often this happens but does not remove it.

seeAlso.why: Cache invalidation strategies on the server side

title: Service Workers and Offline
objectives: Explain where a service worker sits and what it can intercept
Pick a caching strategy per kind of request
Update a service worker without breaking users

cards.title: A programmable proxy in the browser
cards.body: A service worker is a script the browser runs separately from the page. Once installed, it can intercept the page’s network requests for its scope and answer from a cache, from the network, or both. That is what makes offline pages and instant repeat loads possible.

cards.title: Misconception: a service worker replaces HTTP caching
cards.body: The HTTP cache still works underneath. The service worker’s own cache is controlled entirely by your script: nothing expires unless you delete it. A careless cache-first rule can keep serving an old file indefinitely.

cards.title: The service worker lifecycle
cards.body: A new version does not take over pages the old one controls straight away.
steps: Register: the page asks the browser to install the script
Install: cache the files the app shell needs
Waiting: the new version waits while old pages are open
Activate: delete old caches; start controlling pages
Fetch: intercept requests from controlled pages

cards.title: Three strategies cover most requests
cards.body: Cache first suits versioned static files. Network first, falling back to cache, suits pages and API reads that should be fresh when possible. Stale-while-revalidate answers from cache immediately and refreshes the copy in the background, for data where slightly old is acceptable.

cards.title: Trap: caching the HTML cache-first
cards.body: If the app shell HTML is served cache-first, users keep loading the old shell, which references old asset names, until the service worker itself updates. Serve HTML network-first (or revalidate it), and reserve cache-first for hashed assets.

cards.title: Edge case: service worker scope
cards.body: A service worker controls only pages under the path it was served from: a worker at /app/sw.js controls /app/ by default and cannot control /. To control a wider scope, serve the script from that path or send the Service-Worker-Allowed response header. Mis-scoped workers explain many “offline works on some pages only” reports.

questions.prompt: What can a service worker do that a normal page script cannot?

choices.label: Read the DOM of every open tab
Intercept the page’s network requests and answer them
Bypass HTTPS requirements
Run before the browser downloads any HTML for a first-ever visit

questions.explanation: It is a proxy for its scope; it has no DOM access and requires a secure context.

questions.prompt: Which strategy suits app.3f9a1c.js?

choices.label: Never cache
Network first
Network only
Cache first

questions.explanation: The URL changes when the content changes, so the cached copy is always correct.

questions.prompt: You deploy a new service worker. Users have the site open in a tab. When does the new version control that tab by default?

choices.label: Immediately, even in the middle of the user’s session
After all tabs using the old version are closed and the page loads again
Only after the whole browser is restarted
Never: users must clear their cache to get it

questions.explanation: The new version waits so one page is never served by two versions.

questions.prompt: A news list should load instantly and refresh in the background. Which strategy?

choices.label: Network only
Cache first with no expiry
Stale-while-revalidate
Cache only

questions.explanation: Serve cached data now and update the cache for next time.

questions.prompt: Order the service worker lifecycle.

items.label: Wait while old pages are open

questions.explanation: Install and activate are separate so updates are safe.

questions.prompt: Offline support for a field-inspection app used where signal is patchy.
constraints: Data must reach the server eventually

approaches.label: Cache API responses forever, cache first
Cache the app shell, store submissions in IndexedDB, and send them when back online
Network only, with an error message offline

rationaleOptions.label: Queued submissions are sent when the connection returns
The shell and forms work with no signal
Caching API responses forever keeps the data correct

rationaleConflicts.r3: Cached responses never update, so inspectors would see outdated data.

questions.explanation: Offline-first apps cache the shell, queue writes locally and sync later.

flashcards.front: Where does a service worker sit?
flashcards.back: Between the page and the network, for requests in its scope.

flashcards.front: Why does a new version wait?
flashcards.back: So pages are not controlled by two versions at once; it activates when old pages close.
Cache first.

mechanism.title: How a service worker handles requests and updates
steps: A service worker is registered by a page for a scope (a path prefix). It runs on its own thread with no DOM access, only in secure contexts (HTTPS or localhost), and the browser can stop it when idle and start it again for the next event.
On install, it usually opens a named cache and stores the files the app shell needs. If any of those fail to download, installation fails and the previous version stays in charge.

After install, the new version waits until no pages are controlled by the old one. Then it activates, which is the moment to delete caches from old versions. A page can ask the waiting worker to take over sooner, but then it must be ready for a version change mid-session.

For each request in scope, the fetch handler decides what to return: a cached response, a network response, or a combination such as network with a timeout falling back to cache. Requests it does not handle go to the network as usual (through the HTTP cache).

Writes made offline need their own handling: store them (for example in IndexedDB) and replay them when the connection returns, either when the page sees it is online again or through a background sync event where the browser supports it.
The browser checks for an updated service worker script on navigation and periodically. Serving the worker script itself with a short cache lifetime ensures users get updates promptly.

useWhen: Offline-capable apps and repeat-visit speed for apps people return to often.
Cache first for hashed assets; network first or stale-while-revalidate for HTML and data.
avoidWhen: Avoid cache-first for HTML or unversioned files; users can be stuck on old versions.
Avoid caching personal API responses without a plan for logout and expiry.

numbers.title: Repeat-visit load with a cached shell
assumptions: App shell: HTML 30 KB plus 600 KB of assets (example)
Mobile link 2 Mbit/s with 150 ms RTT (example)
Shell cached by the service worker
steps: Without the cache: about 630 KB × 8 = 5,040 kbit ÷ 2,000 kbit/s ≈ 2.5 s of transfer plus round trips.
With cache-first assets: the 600 KB comes from disk, typically in tens of milliseconds.
Network-first HTML still costs a round trip (150 ms) plus 30 KB (0.12 s) when online.
Offline, the HTML falls back to the cached copy, so the app still opens.
numbers.result: Caching the shell turns a multi-second repeat load into roughly one round trip plus local reads, and keeps the app usable offline.

india.title: The service worker lifecycle as documented
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: web.dev’s article on the service worker lifecycle, by Chrome engineers, explains why a new worker waits: if two versions controlled pages at the same time, one page could load assets cached by another version and break. It describes the skip-waiting option and its risk, and recommends cleaning old caches in the activate step, which is the pattern this lesson follows.

pitfalls.trap: “The service worker will keep users up to date.”
pitfalls.say: “Only if I design it to: HTML network-first, hashed assets cache-first, and old caches cleaned on activate.”

pitfalls.trap: “Offline just means caching GET requests.”
pitfalls.say: “Writes made offline must be stored and replayed when the connection returns.”

takeaways: A service worker intercepts requests in its scope and decides cache or network.
New versions install, wait, then activate.
Cache first for hashed files; network first or stale-while-revalidate for HTML and data.
Offline writes need a local queue and a replay.

interactive.title: Why do users see the old version?
interactive.prompt: You deploy a fix. Users with the site open in a tab keep seeing the old version even after reloading once. The service worker serves HTML cache-first.

choices.label: The new worker is waiting, and the old one keeps serving the cached HTML
choices.feedback: Right: the waiting worker cannot take over while the old one controls open pages.

choices.label: The CDN has not updated yet
choices.feedback: Possible in general, but the cache-first HTML in the service worker is enough to explain it.

choices.label: Browsers cache HTML for 24 hours by default
choices.feedback: There is no such fixed default; the service worker’s own cache rule is the cause.

interactive.reveal: Serve HTML network-first, keep the worker script’s HTTP cache short, and clean old caches on activate. Optionally prompt users to reload when a new version is waiting.
